newsitem.title: USA: G7 steps up war of words on rising dollar.
newsitem.headline: G7 steps up war of words on rising dollar.

text.p: The Group of Seven rich industrial nations stepped up its war of words on Sunday aimed at talking financial markets out of driving up the dollar.

Speaking to reporters ahead of a meeting of G7 finance ministers and central bank chiefs, German and Japanese officials made clear they opposed any further weakening of their currencies against the high-flying dollar.
"The Bundesbank is not interested in currency market overshoots. We are in interested in seeing the mark remain a strong international currency," German central bank President Hans Tietmeyer said.

The dollar's buoyancy on world currency markets was among the subjects expected be discussed on Sunday by the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. The meeting, which began after 12:00 p.m EDT (1600 GMT), is expected to last at least until 5:00 p.m. (2100 GMT).

"Japan will make its currency stance clear, that excessive yen weakness as well as excessive yen strength is undesirable, and it will deal decisively with such moves," a Japanese finance ministry official told reporters on Saturday.

Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters after meeting German Finance Minister Theo Waigel ahead of the G7 gathering that they had agreed the group would cooperate to deal with some concerns about the strong dollar.
And Mitsuzuka and U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin agreed at their bilateral meeting on Sunday that the recent weakness of the yen was a source of concern.
Washington is worried that a weak yen will make Japanese products more competitive on world markets, pushing the Asian nation's trade surplus back up to troublesome levels.
At their last meeting in Berlin in February, the G7 acted to stabilise the dollar by saying they thought its weakness of two years ago had been corrected.

But the dollar has since climbed on currency markets, helped by the strength of the U.S. economy and last month's U.S. quarter-point interest rate rise, while the yen and mark have suffered from the weakness of their domestic economies.

G7 members were therefore expected on Sunday to try to reinforce the message that the dollar's rise had gone far enough, without coming out with excessively tough language that might knock it back on currency markets.
The G7 was also expected to focus on Japan, amid U.S. fears that a planned budget squeeze and consumption tax will reduce Japanese imports and swell its trade surplus.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said after a meeting on Friday with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that both had agreed Japan should avoid a big rise in its trade surplus.
European members of the G7 were expected to report on progress towards launching a single European currency in 1999.
Though there is growing belief that monetary union will go ahead on time, those outside Europe still want to hear what the continent is doing to combat mass unemployment and underpin economic growth.
And Africa's economic woes were expected to receive a rare airing at the rich nations' top table.

The United States is looking at opening up trade with Africa, in a move that would coincide with a drive by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to write-off debt owed by poor nations, mostly in Africa,
For the policymakers in the rich world, economic reforms to liberalise African economies would be the best way to lift the continent out of a spiral of conflict and poverty.

But they concede there has to be peace in Zaire, where rebels fighting to oust President Mobutu Sese Seko have overrun two-thirds of the country, before economic reforms can kick in and bring the region into the mainstream of the world economy.
